newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian-U.S. crew circle Mir before risky repairs.
newsitem.headline: Russian-U.S. crew circle Mir before risky repairs.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts and a U.S. astronaut circled the crippled Mir space station in a Soyuz escape capsule for 45 minutes on Friday, filming the exterior in preparation for risky repair work.

Mission Control officials said commander Anatoly Solovyov guided the Soyuz manually back to Mir after British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale filmed the station, which was seriously damaged in an accident on June 25.
"We've touched gently," Solovyov said in a radio link-up, to the evident relief of all at Korolyov Mission Control just outside Moscow.
The three-man crew, which also included flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, reboarded Mir about one hour later after redocking at 6:13 p.m. (1413 GMT).
The new crew is preparing to fix damage done when Mir collided with its cargo ship while redocking in June. The accident was the worst mishap in Mir's 11 years in orbit.
The Soyuz undocked on one side of Mir on Friday and redocked on the opposite side near the Spektr module that was punctured during the June collision.
Redocking near the Spektr means the cosmonauts will be able to make a quick escape if anything goes wrong during the repairs, which will include sealing the Spektr.

Russian flight director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters at Mission Control that Foale had not immediately spotted any holes in Spektr although the pictures will come under closer scrutiny by experts on earth.
"At first glance there were no tears or cracks in Spektr but Michael said there were some very interesting pictures," the flight director said.

Previous commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin returned safely to earth on Thursday after enduring one of the most gruelling six months in the history of human space flight.
The new crew enjoyed a change of luck on Thursday when they repaired the main Elektron oxygen generating system just as the old crew shut the hatch on their Soyuz capsule, officials said.

The Spektr module now is sealed off from the rest of the station. The two Russian cosmonauts will open the hatch next Wednesday to reattach cables linked to Spektr's solar panels to restore the ship's energy system.

To prepare for the Friday Soyuz trip, the crew shut off the oxygen system they had worked so hard to repair. "We turned it on yesterday evening and it worked fine until this morning, and we have turned it off for two reasons," Antoshechkin said.

"One, to lower energy demands on the station during the undocking today," he said. "And second, because it can only be turned off by the crew, and in case that, knock on wood (for luck), the undocking fails, then we couldn't turn it off later."
All three crew members were packed into the Soyuz for Friday's flight because space officials do not want to leave anyone on Mir without an emergency escape vehicle.
On Sunday, Mir will redock with its old Progress resupply ship, the very procedure that caused the June accident. This time the crew expects to do the operation on automatic pilot.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin were undergoing rehabilitation and readjustment to life with gravity on Friday at the Star City cosmonaut training centre outside Moscow, officials said.
Mishaps during their six-month mission include a fire, loss of station's orientation, an irregular heartbeat suffered by Tsibliyev and problems with the power and oxygen supplies.
They face some tough questions about their mission but flight director Solovyov praised their work.
"It was a difficult flight. Some things worked out, some did not. I think the crew deserves an award," he said.
